extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research integrity officers, science journalists, and interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, documenting, and judging research misconduct and breaches of scientific standards (data manipulation, misrepresentation, institutional response) based on investigation reports and primary materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation / shading of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "a disturbing pattern of misrepresentation of results and shading of truth"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report characterizes misrepresentation as presenting results in a way that conceals their true nature. Examples include selective reporting, altering presentation to hide inconsistencies, or describing findings differently than the underlying data warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reckless disregard for basic scientific standards
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad standard covering failures in methodology, record-keeping, transparency, and response to concerns. The post links this wording to repeated instances of cutting corners, pushing analyses toward significance, and other procedural failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altering/changed data to show desired effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee found instances in which Hauser changed data so that it would show a desired effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit data alteration (changing values) that changes statistical outcomes (e.g., moves a result from non-significant to significant) is misconduct. The committee reconstructed analyses to identify such changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushing analyses toward statistical significance (p‑hacking)
rubrics_metrics.description: "pushing analyses of data further in the direction of significance than the actual findings warranted"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulating analysis choices, selectively reporting analyses, or otherwise exploiting analytic flexibility to obtain significance rather than accurately reflecting what the data show. The report cites this as a recurring shortcoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting results as wished rather than as observed
rubrics_metrics.description: "reporting results as he may have wished them to have been, rather than as they actually were."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes wishful or biased reporting from honest reporting. Guidance implies responsibility to report findings faithfully, including null or contradictory results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to take or respond to legitimate lab concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Hauser "rebuffed or downplayed questions and concerns from people in his laboratory about how a result was obtained."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators and PIs should take lab members' concerns seriously, investigate discrepancies, and avoid intimidation or dismissal. Downplaying or rebuffing concerns can enable ongoing misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding fabrication vs. systematic cutting corners (nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: "We did not find evidence that [professor] Hauser has been inventing findings out of whole cloth" — yet there were repeated instances of cutting corners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction: misconduct may be explicit fabrication or a pattern of corner-cutting and manipulation that still invalidates results. Investigations should assess both outright fabrication and systematic malpractice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and provide raw/processed data, procedures, and code
rubrics_metrics.description: The Harvard committee had access to "a huge amount of raw data and of processed data, including a lot of e-mails...multiple copies of all source code, all results of all analyses" enabling detailed reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough records (raw data, processed datasets, analysis scripts, instruction sheets, emails) are essential for transparency and post-hoc reconstruction. Lack of such materials obstructs adjudication and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough, painstaking reconstruction of analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee "painstakingly reconstructed the process of data analysis" and debunked excuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should reconstruct analytic workflows, re-run analyses, and check provenance of numbers; such work is necessary to determine whether results reflect real data or altered analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional responsibility to prevent and address bullying/retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions raised about whether laboratory members were bullied and what their employer did, given a legal obligation to prevent such action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must investigate allegations of bullying/retaliation, protect whistleblowers, and take remedial action; failure to do so can silence honest reporting and enable misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about investigative process and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion about redaction of committee names and Harvard's unwillingness to post the report; some commenters recommend publishing case studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance privacy/legal concerns with public need for transparency. Publishing investigation reports, with appropriate redactions, and documenting methods used in inquiries helps the community learn and deter misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate corrective actions and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Hauser resigned in 2011 and was found guilty of misconduct by ORI in 2012; commenters note retractions and consequences at other cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings of misconduct should lead to proportionate consequences (retraction, correction, sanctions) and consideration of ongoing publication with collaborators; accountability restores trust and corrects the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerns about continued publishing with prominent co‑authors after findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted that "Hauser is back publishing in the scientific literature, with a number of luminaries as co-authors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community and co-authors should consider the ethical implications of collaborating with researchers found to have committed misconduct; vigilance about contribution, data provenance, and potential reputational effects is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about overreliance on 'statistical significance' as sole criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments discuss statistical significance as 'an important criterion' but also as potentially deceptive or manipulable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical significance should not be the sole arbiter of truth; robustness, transparency of analysis choices, effect sizes, and reproducibility matter. Overemphasis can incentivize manipulation.
